newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kabila's Congo rejects U.N. probe charges.
newsitem.headline: Kabila's Congo rejects U.N. probe charges.

text.p: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has dismissed as untrue a U.N. report which accused Laurent Kabila's government of massacring Rwandan Hutu refugees.
Government spokesman Raphael Ghenda accused the authors of the report, released at the United Nations on Friday, of trying to tarnish the image of the new authorities in Kinshasa.
"There have been many reports of this kind which have proved particularly eccentric. It's a move which is more inclined to causing harm than telling the truth," Ghenda told Reuters.
"It's the work of those who tried in vain to hinder our liberation struggle. This is all they can do now," he added.
The report by a U.N. investigator banned by the Kinshasa government has pointed to 134 separate massacres of Rwandan refugees by forces allied to Kabila in the civil war which brought him to power.
Roberto Garreton of Chile said evidence appeared to point to genocide and systematic executions. He suggested the perpetrators should appear before an international war crimes tribunal.
He also said killings and other grave human rights violations had not stopped after Kabila became president of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as the ex-Zaire is now called.

His new U.N. Human Rights Commission report did not estimate how many people were killed but said eyewitnesses and U.N. relief workers gave evidence of more than 180 incidents of massacres in the former Zaire.
Alliance forces seized power in Kinshasa in May, deposing veteran president Mobutu Sese Seko, after a whirlwind military campaign across the vast Central African state.
Kabila, who declared himself president, denied Garreton's charges and refused to allow the Chilean access.

Over a million Hutus in 1994 crossed into what was then Zaire fearing reprisals for the genocide in Rwanda of minority Tutsis by Hutu hard-liners. The bulk returned home, but U.N. relief officials say up to 200,000 remain unaccounted for.

Hutu militants had used the camps as havens to rebuild their strength and conduct guerrilla raids against the Rwanda government, controlled by Tutsis who were instrumental in the rebellion against Mobutu.
A U.N. investigating team is due to arrive soon in the new Congo for a thorough probe into the alleged massacres.
But the government and the U.N. are still at odds on the timing of the investigation.
The government insists the U.N. probe include the killings carried out under Mobutu. The U.N. wants to focus on Kabila's seven-month bush war.
